title: BPH and Male LUTS: Confirm the Syndrome Before Escalating Therapy
bottomLine: Male lower urinary tract symptoms are not automatically BPH. Confirm the storage/voiding pattern, exclude infection, retention, neurologic disease, medication effects and concerning hematuria/prostate features, then match therapy to symptom burden, prostate-related progression risk and patient goals.
recognize: Voiding symptoms include weak stream, hesitancy, intermittency and incomplete emptying; storage symptoms include urgency, frequency and nocturia.
Acute urinary retention, recurrent infection, renal impairment from obstruction or gross hematuria changes the urgency.
differentiate: Overactive bladder, urethral stricture, prostatitis, bladder cancer, neurogenic bladder, constipation and medication effects can mimic or coexist with BPH.
PSA can support prostate-cancer risk assessment and estimate prostate volume in selected men; it does not diagnose BPH by itself.
assessment: Assess symptom severity/bother, voiding vs storage predominance, retention history, infection/hematuria, constipation, neurologic symptoms, medications, blood pressure and sexual function.
Perform focused abdominal/genitourinary examination and DRE when clinically appropriate.
workup: Use urinalysis and selected PSA/renal function/post-void residual according to presentation and shared decision-making; imaging/cystoscopy are targeted to complications or alternate diagnoses rather than routine in uncomplicated LUTS.
management: Use watchful waiting/lifestyle measures for mild symptoms; alpha blockers improve symptoms, while 5-alpha-reductase inhibitors are most useful when prostate enlargement/progression risk makes them appropriate.
Refer for recurrent retention, renal compromise, recurrent infection, stones, persistent gross hematuria, refractory symptoms or procedural consideration.
medicationSafety: Alpha blockers can cause orthostatic hypotension and falls; review antihypertensives and cataract-surgery history.
5-alpha-reductase inhibitors affect PSA interpretation and can cause sexual adverse effects; document baseline and treatment context.
redFlags: Concerning prostate examination or rapidly progressive symptoms
counselling: Explain that symptom relief and prevention of progression are different goals and may require different therapies.
followUp: Reassess symptom burden, blood pressure/adverse effects, retention risk and response after treatment changes.
examTrap: Calling every older man's nocturia BPH without checking diabetes, sleep apnea, edema/diuretics or overactive bladder.
oneLinePearl: Male LUTS is a syndrome; BPH is one cause, not the default diagnosis.
sourceBasis: Canadian Urological Association guideline: Male LUTS/BPH

title: Urinary Incontinence: Identify the Type Before Choosing Treatment
bottomLine: Urinary incontinence is treated by subtype and cause. Distinguish stress, urgency, mixed, overflow and functional incontinence, look for reversible contributors and retention, then use bladder/pelvic-floor and medication/procedural options that fit the physiology.
recognize: Stress leakage occurs with cough/exertion; urgency incontinence follows a compelling urge; overflow suggests incomplete emptying; functional incontinence reflects mobility/cognition/environment barriers.
differentiate: Dysuria/fever suggests infection; continuous leakage can suggest fistula; new neurologic deficits or saddle symptoms raise neurogenic/cauda-equina concern.
assessment: Ask triggers, urgency, frequency, nocturia, volume, bowel habits, obstetric/pelvic surgery history, mobility/cognition, fluid/caffeine, medications and impact on quality of life.
Use bladder diary and pelvic/neurologic examination when helpful.
workup: Urinalysis is appropriate when infection/hematuria is possible; measure post-void residual when retention/overflow, neurologic disease or treatment risk makes it relevant.
Urodynamics and imaging are reserved for complex/uncertain or refractory cases.
management: Pelvic-floor muscle training is core for stress/mixed incontinence; bladder training and urgency strategies are core for urgency syndromes.
Treat constipation, mobility/environment barriers and offending medications before adding drug burden; refer for prolapse, fistula, major retention or procedural/surgical management.
medicationSafety: Antimuscarinics can worsen dry mouth, constipation, cognition and urinary retention; beta-3 agonists can affect blood pressure and require patient-specific review.
redFlags: New neurologic deficits or saddle anesthesia
counselling: Use non-stigmatizing language and explain that incontinence is common but not an inevitable part of aging.
followUp: Track episodes, function, adverse effects and post-void residual when clinically indicated.
examTrap: Starting an antimuscarinic in a patient with overflow symptoms and a large residual without recognizing retention.
oneLinePearl: First name the incontinence mechanism; then treat it.
sourceBasis: Canadian Urological Association female/functional urology guidance

title: Overactive Bladder: Urgency First, Retention Excluded
bottomLine: Overactive bladder is urgency, usually with frequency/nocturia and sometimes urgency incontinence, after infection and important alternate causes are excluded. Start with bladder training and reversible contributors; use pharmacotherapy only after checking retention, cognition, blood pressure and medication burden.
recognize: Urgency is the defining symptom; frequency/nocturia without urgency may reflect polyuria, sleep disorder, edema redistribution or other causes.
differentiate: UTI, bladder stone/tumour, interstitial cystitis/bladder pain, poorly controlled diabetes, diuretics and outlet obstruction can mimic urgency/frequency.
assessment: Use bladder diary, urinalysis when indicated, fluid/caffeine review, bowel history, pelvic/prostate/neurologic context and medication review.
workup: Measure post-void residual when retention risk, neurologic disease, prior pelvic surgery or obstructive symptoms make it relevant; routine cystoscopy/urodynamics are not needed for uncomplicated presentation.
management: Use bladder training, timed voiding, pelvic-floor strategies and management of constipation/fluid timing first.

If medication is needed, select antimuscarinic or beta-3 agonist according to cognition, constipation, glaucoma/retention risk, blood pressure, interactions and preference; refractory disease may need urology/urogynecology procedures.
medicationSafety: Avoid worsening retention or cognitive burden in frail older adults; monitor blood pressure with beta-3 agonists when relevant.
counselling: Set realistic goals around urgency control and function rather than promising complete symptom elimination.
followUp: Reassess symptom diary, adverse effects, adherence and residual/retention risk after treatment changes.
examTrap: Diagnosing OAB from nocturia alone in a patient with edema and untreated sleep apnea.
oneLinePearl: OAB is an urgency syndrome, not a synonym for frequent urination.
sourceBasis: Canadian Urological Association overactive bladder guidance

title: Erectile Dysfunction: Sexual Symptom, Vascular Clue, Medication Review
bottomLine: Erectile dysfunction is a clinical syndrome with vascular, neurologic, endocrine, medication and psychosexual contributors. Evaluate cardiovascular risk and reversible causes, then use shared decision-making for PDE5 inhibitors and alternatives; nitrates plus PDE5 inhibitors are unsafe.
recognize: Gradual persistent ED with vascular risk factors suggests endothelial disease; situational variability and preserved spontaneous erections can support a psychogenic component but do not exclude medical causes.
differentiate: Low libido points toward androgen/psychological/systemic causes, while ED is specifically failure to achieve/maintain erection sufficient for desired sexual activity.
assessment: Assess onset, erections, libido, relationship/context, diabetes, cardiovascular disease, smoking, sleep apnea, neurologic disease, pelvic surgery, medications/substances and depression/anxiety.
Review exercise tolerance/cardiovascular symptoms before sexual-activity advice in high-risk patients.
workup: Use targeted glucose/A1C, lipids and morning testosterone when symptoms/risk support it; additional endocrine/vascular testing is selective rather than routine.
management: Address vascular risk, medication contributors and relationship/psychological factors; PDE5 inhibitors are first-line for many patients when not contraindicated.
Refer refractory cases, penile deformity, major endocrine abnormality or complex post-surgical disease to urology/sexual medicine.
medicationSafety: PDE5 inhibitors must not be combined with nitrates because profound hypotension can occur; review alpha-blocker timing, blood pressure and CYP interactions.
counselling: Frame ED as a common health issue and possible vascular-risk marker rather than a performance failure.
followUp: Reassess efficacy, adverse effects, adherence/use technique and cardiovascular risk-factor management.
examTrap: Prescribing a PDE5 inhibitor without asking about nitrates or cardiovascular stability.
oneLinePearl: ED can be an early vascular signal; treat the person, not just the erection.
sourceBasis: Canadian Urological Association erectile dysfunction guidance

title: Prostatitis: Acute Infection, Chronic Pelvic Pain, or Something Else?
bottomLine: Prostatitis is not one disease. Acute bacterial prostatitis is a systemic urinary infection with possible sepsis/retention; chronic bacterial prostatitis and chronic pelvic pain syndrome require different diagnostic and treatment strategies. Avoid vigorous prostatic massage in acutely ill patients.
recognize: Acute bacterial prostatitis can cause fever, dysuria, pelvic/perineal pain, obstructive symptoms and a tender prostate.
Chronic pelvic pain syndrome may have pelvic/ejaculatory pain and urinary symptoms without proven bacterial infection.
differentiate: Pyelonephritis, epididymo-orchitis, urethritis/STI, stone, abscess and urinary retention can overlap clinically.
assessment: Assess sepsis, retention, sexual/STI history, instrumentation, recurrent UTI, immunocompromise and medication/allergy history.
workup: Obtain urinalysis/culture before antibiotics when feasible without delaying treatment in an unstable patient; STI testing is exposure/syndrome driven.
Imaging is indicated when abscess, obstruction or failure to improve is suspected.
management: Treat acute bacterial prostatitis with appropriate systemic antibiotics and escalation for sepsis, retention, vomiting or abscess concern; chronic pelvic pain requires multimodal symptom/functional management rather than repeated empiric antibiotics without infection evidence.
medicationSafety: Select antibiotics using culture, penetration, renal function, interactions and local resistance; avoid unnecessary prolonged fluoroquinolone exposure when the diagnosis is unsupported.
redFlags: Failure to improve on appropriate therapy
counselling: Explain the difference between bacterial infection and chronic pelvic pain so recurrent symptoms do not automatically trigger another antibiotic course.
followUp: Review cultures, symptom response and recurrent infection evaluation; persistent or complicated cases need urology.
examTrap: Repeatedly treating chronic pelvic pain with antibiotics despite negative infection evidence.
oneLinePearl: Acute prostatitis is an infection syndrome; chronic pelvic pain is not automatically infection.
sourceBasis: Choosing Wisely Canada antimicrobial stewardship principles

title: Testicular and Scrotal Disorders: Torsion First in Acute Pain
bottomLine: Sudden unilateral scrotal pain is testicular torsion until excluded. Do not delay urgent surgical/urologic assessment for a reassuring urinalysis or for imaging when clinical suspicion is high; slower presentations require evaluation for epididymitis, hernia, hydrocele/varicocele, tumour and referred pain.
recognize: Torsion often presents with abrupt severe pain, nausea/vomiting, high-riding or abnormal testicular lie and absent cremasteric reflex, but no single sign is perfectly sensitive.
Epididymitis is more often gradual and may have urinary/STI features; testicular cancer commonly presents as a painless mass.
differentiate: Torsion, incarcerated hernia and Fournier gangrene are time-critical; hydrocele/varicocele are usually non-emergent unless the pattern changes.
assessment: Assess onset/time course, trauma, urinary/STI symptoms, systemic illness and full abdominal/inguinal/scrotal examination.
workup: Doppler ultrasound is useful when it can be obtained promptly without delaying definitive care in an equivocal case; urine/STI testing supports alternative diagnoses but cannot rule out torsion.
management: Activate urgent urologic/surgical pathway for suspected torsion; treat epididymitis according to likely pathogens/exposure and evaluate persistent masses with ultrasound/urology.
medicationSafety: Do not mask diagnostic delay with analgesia-only discharge when torsion remains plausible; analgesia should be given while urgent evaluation proceeds.
redFlags: Systemic toxicity or necrotizing skin change
counselling: Teach that sudden recurrent scrotal pain still requires urgent assessment even if it resolves spontaneously because intermittent torsion can occur.
followUp: Ensure resolution/follow-up of epididymitis and prompt urology for persistent mass or recurrent pain.
examTrap: Waiting for urine results or routine imaging when the presentation strongly suggests torsion.
oneLinePearl: Acute scrotal pain is a clock: torsion gets excluded before benign labels are assigned.
sourceBasis: Canadian Urological Association/Pediatric Urologists of Canada educational guidance

title: Renal Imaging: Choose the Modality That Answers the Question
bottomLine: Renal imaging is question-specific. Ultrasound is useful for hydronephrosis, retention and many structural questions; noncontrast CT is highly sensitive for many stones; contrast CT/MRI answer different mass/vascular/infectious questions. Do not order serial imaging without a management question.
recognize: Hydronephrosis is a structural finding, not a diagnosis; obstruction significance depends on symptoms, infection, kidney function and cause.
Simple cysts differ from complex cystic or solid masses that require risk-based characterization.
differentiate: Flank pain with pregnancy or radiation concern often starts with ultrasound; suspected renal colic in a nonpregnant adult may require noncontrast CT depending on severity/diagnostic uncertainty.
Contrast imaging may be essential when renal mass, vascular disease, abscess or complicated infection is suspected.
assessment: Define the clinical question first: stone, obstruction, mass, infection, renovascular disease, trauma or chronic structural disease.
Review pregnancy, kidney function, contrast allergy history and prior imaging.
workup: Select ultrasound, CT or MRI based on the question and avoid duplicate imaging that will not change management.
Interpret imaging alongside urinalysis, kidney function and symptoms; incidental findings need a documented follow-up plan when appropriate.
management: Obstructed infected systems require urgent drainage/source-control pathways; suspicious masses or progressive hydronephrosis require urology/appropriate specialty referral.
medicationSafety: Contrast decisions should balance diagnostic benefit against current kidney function and other risk; do not deny necessary imaging from an outdated blanket 'contrast nephropathy' rule.
redFlags: Rapid kidney-function decline with structural concern
counselling: Explain why a specific imaging test is being chosen and what result would change the plan.
followUp: Close the loop on incidental masses/cysts, hydronephrosis and repeat imaging intervals when indicated.
examTrap: Ordering contrast CT for every renal complaint—or avoiding necessary contrast imaging categorically without weighing the diagnostic need.
oneLinePearl: Renal imaging starts with the question, not the machine.
sourceBasis: Canadian Urological Association imaging practice resources

title: Urinalysis in Renal Disease: Sediment, Protein, and Context
bottomLine: Urinalysis is a pattern tool, not a diagnosis. Interpret dipstick with microscopy, symptoms and kidney function: blood/protein/casts can signal glomerular disease, while pyuria/bacteriuria requires a compatible clinical syndrome before antibiotics are justified.
recognize: Protein plus dysmorphic RBCs/RBC casts supports glomerular disease; WBC casts can suggest renal parenchymal inflammation/infection; hyaline casts can be nonspecific.
Dipstick blood can reflect RBCs, hemoglobin or myoglobin; microscopy clarifies whether RBCs are actually present.
differentiate: Asymptomatic bacteriuria is not the same as UTI in most nonpregnant populations.
Transient protein can occur with illness/exercise; persistent albuminuria/proteinuria needs quantification and chronic disease evaluation.
assessment: Link UA to symptoms, BP, edema, systemic disease, medication exposure, menstruation/collection contamination and kidney-function trend.
workup: Confirm/quantify persistent protein with ACR/PCR as appropriate; culture urine when the result will affect treatment; use microscopy for suspected glomerular/interstitial disease.
Repeat a contaminated or transiently abnormal sample rather than overdiagnosing chronic disease from one poor specimen.
management: Treat the syndrome and underlying disease, not the urinalysis line item; nephritic sediment, heavy proteinuria or renal decline warrants nephrology evaluation.
medicationSafety: Do not prescribe antibiotics for pyuria/bacteriuria without a compatible indication; unnecessary treatment causes adverse effects and resistance.
redFlags: Pregnancy with clinically significant urinary findings
counselling: Explain specimen collection and why an abnormal dipstick may need confirmation before it means disease.
followUp: Close the loop on persistent hematuria/proteinuria and repeat testing after transient illness when appropriate.
examTrap: Treating pyuria as UTI or dipstick blood as confirmed hematuria without clinical/microscopic context.
oneLinePearl: Urinalysis tells a pattern story; symptoms and microscopy decide what it means.

title: Acid–Base Disorders: Primary Process, Compensation, Mixed Disorder
bottomLine: Acid–base interpretation is a sequence: assess pH, identify the primary respiratory/metabolic process, judge expected compensation, calculate the anion gap when metabolic acidosis is present, and ask whether a mixed disorder fits the patient. Treat the cause, not the pH label alone.
recognize: Metabolic acidosis can reflect lactate, ketoacids, renal failure, toxins or bicarbonate loss; respiratory acidosis reflects inadequate effective ventilation; alkaloses require their own volume/chloride, endocrine, pulmonary or toxicologic differential.
differentiate: A near-normal pH can hide two opposing primary disorders.
Compensation does not normally overcorrect the pH; an unexpected CO2 or bicarbonate response should trigger mixed-disorder reasoning.
assessment: Assess ventilation, oxygenation, perfusion, hemodynamics, mental status, GI losses, renal function, diabetes/ketones, sepsis, toxin/medication exposure and pregnancy.
workup: Use blood gas with electrolytes and anion gap; add lactate, ketones, toxicology, urine studies or imaging according to the syndrome.
Trend after therapy when ongoing physiologic instability is present.
management: Restore ventilation/perfusion, correct DKA/sepsis/toxin/renal/GI causes and treat dangerous electrolyte abnormalities.
Bicarbonate or renal-replacement therapy is reserved for selected indications and is not a universal response to low pH.
medicationSafety: Insulin, diuretics, saline/chloride load, bicarbonate, sedatives/opioids and toxin antidotes can all change acid–base physiology and require monitoring.
redFlags: Severe renal failure or refractory electrolyte disturbance
counselling: For chronic disorders, explain the underlying disease and medication/sick-day plan rather than focusing on the blood-gas number.
followUp: Repeat blood gas/electrolytes when treatment response or ongoing instability requires it; avoid serial gases without a clinical question.
examTrap: Calling a normal pH 'normal acid–base status' when CO2 and bicarbonate show opposing severe abnormalities.
oneLinePearl: Primary process, expected compensation, then mixed disorder—always in that order.
